title: Confidently wrong
text: The less competent people are, the less likely they are to know it — a finding that has entered popular culture as the Dunning-Kruger effect. In the original 1999 experiments, students who scored lowest on tests of humour, grammar and logic {{1}} their performance most severely, while the top performers actually {{2}} themselves, assuming that tasks they found easy must be easy for everyone. The explanation is {{3}} simple: the same knowledge you need to answer well is the knowledge you need to realise you are answering badly. If you cannot tell a valid argument from an invalid one, you cannot {{4}} your own argument's validity either. Skill, in other words, contains its own measuring stick, and the unskilled have no {{5}} of it. The good news is that the effect is a nudge, not a destiny: studies show that even a brief training session, or a small {{6}} of the right knowledge, lets people assess themselves far more accurately. The internet age has given the effect new {{7}} — comment sections are not short of confident amateurs — but psychologists caution against its popular misuse, which tends to be {{8}} on whoever disagrees with us. The honest conclusion is symmetrical: we are all blind to something, and wisdom starts by admitting where.

gaps.explanation: 'students who scored lowest overestimated their performance most severely' — rated it too high; admire would praise it, and miss and ignore do not rate it at all.
'the top performers actually underestimated themselves' — rated themselves too low; the under- forms are traps.
'deceptively simple' — simpler than it looks; the passage's irony needs exactly this adverb.
'you cannot judge your own argument's validity' — assess it; jumble = mix up, jeer = mock.
'the unskilled have no inkling of it' — no faint idea; inclination takes 'to', incidence is for rates of events.
'a small dose of the right knowledge' — a measured amount, as of medicine; doze = a short sleep.
'given the effect new relevance' — made it matter again; reverence = deep respect, referendum = a public vote.
'tends to be invoked on whoever disagrees' — called into play against them; evoke = summon a feeling, revoke = cancel.
